claim: XRCC4 and DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4) form a tight complex that provides DNA ligase activity for classical non-homologous end joining.
source: XRCC4 and DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4) form a tight complex that provides DNA ligase activity for classical non-homologous end joining (the predominant DNA double-strand break repair pathway in higher eukaryotes) and is stimulated by XLF.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about XRCC4 and LIG4 function in DNA repair.

claim: Classical non-homologous end joining is the predominant DNA double-strand break repair pathway in higher eukaryotes.
source: XRCC4 and DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4) form a tight complex that provides DNA ligase activity for classical non-homologous end joining (the predominant DNA double-strand break repair pathway in higher eukaryotes) and is stimulated by XLF.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA repair pathways in eukaryotes.

claim: XLF stimulates the XRCC4/LIG4 complex.
source: XRCC4 and DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4) form a tight complex that provides DNA ligase activity for classical non-homologous end joining (the predominant DNA double-strand break repair pathway in higher eukaryotes) and is stimulated by XLF.
evidence: This is established knowledge about XLF's role in c-NHEJ.

claim: XLF associates with XRCC4 to form filaments that bridge DNA independently of LIG4.
source: Independently of LIG4, XLF also associates with XRCC4 to form filaments that bridge DNA.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript and confirmed by the experimental data presented.

claim: XRCC4/XLF complexes rapidly load and connect broken DNA.
source: These XRCC4/XLF complexes rapidly load and connect broken DNA, thereby stimulating intermolecular ligation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript showing DNA bridging activity.

claim: XRCC4/XLF complexes stimulate intermolecular ligation.
source: These XRCC4/XLF complexes rapidly load and connect broken DNA, thereby stimulating intermolecular ligation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T4 DNA ligase assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: XRCC4 and XLF both include disordered C-terminal tails.
source: XRCC4 and XLF both include disordered C-terminal tails that are functionally dispensable in isolation but are phosphorylated in response to DNA damage by DNA-PK and/or ATM.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about these proteins.

claim: The C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF are functionally dispensable in isolation.
source: XRCC4 and XLF both include disordered C-terminal tails that are functionally dispensable in isolation but are phosphorylated in response to DNA damage by DNA-PK and/or ATM.
evidence: This is based on prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF are phosphorylated in response to DNA damage by DNA-PK and/or ATM.
source: XRCC4 and XLF both include disordered C-terminal tails that are functionally dispensable in isolation but are phosphorylated in response to DNA damage by DNA-PK and/or ATM.
evidence: This is supported by prior research and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Fourteen phosphorylation sites in XRCC4 and XLF were concomitantly modified by substituting them with either alanine or aspartate residues.
source: Here we concomitantly modify the tails of XRCC4 and XLF by substituting fourteen previously identified phosphorylation sites with either alanine or aspartate residues.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations impact the stability of XRCC4/XLF complexes.
source: These phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations impact both the stability and DNA bridging capacity of XRCC4/XLF complexes, but without affecting their ability to stimulate LIG4 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR and ITC experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations impact the DNA bridging capacity of XRCC4/XLF complexes.
source: These phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations impact both the stability and DNA bridging capacity of XRCC4/XLF complexes, but without affecting their ability to stimulate LIG4 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA bridging assays and T4 ligase assays in the manuscript.

claim: Phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations do not affect the ability of XRCC4/XLF complexes to stimulate LIG4 activity.
source: These phospho-blocking and -mimicking mutations impact both the stability and DNA bridging capacity of XRCC4/XLF complexes, but without affecting their ability to stimulate LIG4 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LIG4 ligation assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: Phosphorylation may regulate DNA bridging by XRCC4/XLF filaments.
source: Implicit in this finding is that phosphorylation may regulate DNA bridging by XRCC4/XLF filaments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects of phospho-mimicking mutations.

claim: In mammalian cells, classical non-homologous end joining (c-NHEJ) is the primary pathway that repairs DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: In mammalian cells, classical non-homologous end joining (c-NHEJ) is the primary pathway that repairs DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA repair.

claim: The c-NHEJ pathway is specialized in the repair of two-ended DSBs like those induced by ionizing radiation or radiomimetic drugs.
source: This pathway is specialized in the repair of two-ended DSBs like those that are induced by ionizing radiation or by many radiomimetic drugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about c-NHEJ specificity.

claim: The c-NHEJ pathway is exploited by developing lymphocytes to repair DSBs introduced by the RAG1/2 endonuclease during V(D)J gene rearrangement.
source: The c-NHEJ pathway is also exploited by developing lymphocytes to repair DSBs that are introduced by the RAG1/2 endonuclease during antibody and T-cell receptor V(D)J gene rearrangement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about V(D)J recombination.

claim: The c-NHEJ machinery is versatile and adapts to efficiently repair DSBs with diverse DNA end structures.
source: The c-NHEJ machinery is versatile and adapts to efficiently repair DSBs with diverse DNA end structures (Lieber, 2010; Reid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Core c-NHEJ effectors include the heterodimeric Ku DNA end sensor, DNA-PKcs, DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4), and the structurally related XRCC4 and XLF proteins.
source: Core c-NHEJ effectors include the heterodimeric Ku DNA end sensor, the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs), DNA Ligase 4 (LIG4), and the structurally related XRCC4 and XLF proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about c-NHEJ components.

claim: Ku performs the recognition step in c-NHEJ, rapidly and avidly binding and protecting broken DNA ends.
source: (1) Ku performs the recognition step, rapidly and avidly binding and protecting broken DNA ends
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ku function in c-NHEJ.

claim: Ku recruits DNA-PKcs and promotes DNA end synapsis, regulating DNA end access.
source: (2) Ku recruits DNA-PKcs and promotes DNA end synapsis, regulating DNA end access
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sequential model of c-NHEJ.

claim: DNA end processing in c-NHEJ is carried out by non-core factors including Artemis, X-family polymerases, or other DNA modifying enzymes.
source: (3) if required, DNA end processing is carried on by non-core factors (Artemis, X-family polymerases, or other DNA modifying enzymes)
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA end processing in c-NHEJ.

claim: The LIG4/XRCC4 complex, assisted by XLF, catalyzes the ligation step of c-NHEJ directly.
source: 4] the LIG4/XRCC4 complex, assisted by XLF, catalyzes the ligation step directly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ligation step in c-NHEJ.

claim: LIG4, XRCC4 and XLF form filamentous structures that bridge DNA and promote ligation in vitro.
source: These paradigm shifting data include structural, biochemical, and functional studies revealing that LIG4, XRCC4 and XLF form filamentous structures that bridge DNA and promote ligation in vitro (Andres et al., 2012; Hammel et al., 2011; Ropars et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2015, 2012; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: XRCC4/XLF filaments rapidly and robustly 'splint' broken DNA as 'sleeve-like' protein bandages.
source: This DNA tethering, which has been observed in vitro, implies an early function for XRCC4/XLF filaments during DNA repair; we have proposed that XRCC4/XLF complexes rapidly and robustly 'splint' broken DNA as 'sleeve-like' protein bandages (Brouwer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on cited research.

claim: In living cells, XRCC4 and XLF, independently of LIG4, form filamentous super-structures at bleomycin-induced DSBs that adopt various configurations.
source: In fact, a recent study showed that in living cells, XRCC4 and XLF, independently of LIG4, form filamentous super-structures at bleomycin-induced DSBs that adopt various configurations (Reid et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Specifically disrupting XRCC4-XLF filament formation by mutagenesis affects c-NHEJ function in living cells.
source: However, specifically disrupting XRCC4-XLF filament formation (by mutagenesis) affects c-NHEJ function in living cells (Roy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Nine phosphorylation sites were identified in XRCC4.
source: Briefly, we identified nine phosphorylation sites in XRCC4 (Yu et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors.

claim: Six phosphorylation sites were identified in XLF.
source: Lees-Miller and colleagues identified six sites in XLF (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on cited research.

claim: Eight of the nine sites in XRCC4 (residues S193, S260, S304, S315, S320, T323, S327, and S328) are phosphorylated in vivo.
source: Studies using phospho-specific antibodies and numerous phospho-proteome reports have confirmed that eight of the nine sites (residues S193, S260, S304, S315, S320, T323, S327, and S328 – using UniProt Q13426 isoform 1 as reference) in XRCC4 and minimally four of the six sites (residues S132, S203, S245 and S251 – using UniProt Q9H9Q4 isoform 1 as reference) in XLF are phosphorylated in vivo (http://www.phosphosite.org).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-specific antibodies and phospho-proteome databases.

claim: Minimally four of the six sites in XLF (residues S132, S203, S245 and S251) are phosphorylated in vivo.
source: Studies using phospho-specific antibodies and numerous phospho-proteome reports have confirmed that eight of the nine sites (residues S193, S260, S304, S315, S320, T323, S327, and S328 – using UniProt Q13426 isoform 1 as reference) in XRCC4 and minimally four of the six sites (residues S132, S203, S245 and S251 – using UniProt Q9H9Q4 isoform 1 as reference) in XLF are phosphorylated in vivo (http://www.phosphosite.org).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-specific antibodies and phospho-proteome databases.

claim: All the phosphorylation sites in XRCC4 and XLF are located in the C-terminal tails.
source: Remarkably, all the above-mentioned phosphorylation sites are located in the C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural diagrams in Figure 1.

claim: XRCC4 and XLF cooperatively form super-complexes detectable by EMSA.
source: Overall, analyses of the activity of the WT proteins confirmed that XRCC4 and XLF cooperatively form super-complexes detectable by EMSA (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: XRCC4 and XLF strongly promote intermolecular DNA cohesive and blunt end ligation.
source: Overall, analyses of the activity of the WT proteins confirmed that XRCC4 and XLF cooperatively form super-complexes detectable by EMSA (Figure 2A and B) that strongly promote intermolecular DNA cohesive and blunt end ligation (Figure 2C,D and E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by T4 DNA ligase assays shown in Figure 2C, D, and E.

claim: XRCC4 and XLF favor molecular collision rates during ligation through robust DNA bridging activity.
source: Overall, analyses of the activity of the WT proteins confirmed that XRCC4 and XLF cooperatively form super-complexes detectable by EMSA (Figure 2A and B) that strongly promote intermolecular DNA cohesive and blunt end ligation (Figure 2C,D and E), by favoring molecular collision rates during ligation through a robust DNA bridging activity as can be seen in Figure 2F and G.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA bridging assays shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: XLF has an intrinsic DNA bridging activity that depends on the presence of its C-terminal tail.
source: In the latter experiment, it can be also observed that XLF has an intrinsic DNA bridging activity that depends on the presence of its C-terminal tail (Figure 2G, lanes 3 and 5, XLF (1-224) lacks the 75 C-terminal residues).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing full-length XLF with the truncated XLF(1-224) variant in Figure 2G.

claim: XLF's intrinsic DNA bridging activity is strongly stimulated by XRCC4.
source: This intrinsic XLF DNA bridging activity is strongly stimulated by XRCC4 (Figure 2G, lanes 3 and 7)
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing XLF alone versus XLF with XRCC4 in Figure 2G.

claim: XLF's DNA bridging stimulation by XRCC4 depends on physical interaction between XLF and XRCC4.
source: This intrinsic XLF DNA bridging activity is strongly stimulated by XRCC4 (Figure 2G, lanes 3 and 7) in a manner that depends on physical interaction between XLF and XRCC4, as tested using an XLF mutant (L115D) described previously that does not interact with XRCC4 but has an intact C-terminal tail (Figure 2G, lanes 4 and 8, Malivert et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated using the XLF L115D mutant that cannot interact with XRCC4, shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Neither the intrinsic DNA binding of XRCC4 nor its ability to form super-complexes with XLF-WT is affected by phospho-blocking eight sites in XRCC4.
source: Neither the intrinsic DNA binding of XRCC4 nor its ability to form super-complexes with XLF-WT is affected by phospho-blocking eight sites in XRCC4 (Figure 3A, XRCC4-Ala).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phospho-mimicking eight sites in XRCC4 strongly reduces XRCC4's intrinsic DNA binding.
source: In contrast, phospho-mimicking these eight sites in XRCC4 strongly reduces XRCC4's intrinsic DNA binding and modestly reduces cooperative DNA binding with XLF-WT (Figure 3A, XRCC4-Asp).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phospho-mimicking eight sites in XRCC4 modestly reduces cooperative DNA binding with XLF-WT.
source: In contrast, phospho-mimicking these eight sites in XRCC4 strongly reduces XRCC4's intrinsic DNA binding and modestly reduces cooperative DNA binding with XLF-WT (Figure 3A, XRCC4-Asp).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neither phospho-blocking nor phospho-mimicking six sites in XLF alters the intrinsic DNA binding activity of XLF.
source: Neither phospho-blocking nor phospho-mimicking six sites in XLF alters either the intrinsic DNA binding activity of XLF or its ability to cooperatively form super-complexes with XRCC4-WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Neither phospho-blocking nor phospho-mimicking six sites in XLF alters its ability to cooperatively form super-complexes with XRCC4-WT.
source: Neither phospho-blocking nor phospho-mimicking six sites in XLF alters either the intrinsic DNA binding activity of XLF or its ability to cooperatively form super-complexes with XRCC4-WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The XRCC4 and XLF variants interact at the protein-protein level similarly to WT XRCC4 and XLF in the absence of DNA.
source: Protein-protein cross-linking experiments in the absence of DNA suggest that the XRCC4 and XLF variants interact at the protein-protein level similarly to WT XRCC4 and XLF (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The dissociation constant values (Kd) for WT-WT, Ala-Ala, and Asp-Asp XRCC4-XLF combinations are equal within experimental errors and are approximately 2 μM.
source: The dissociation constant values (Kd) obtained for the three different combinations (WT-WT, Ala-Ala, and Asp-Asp) are equal within the experimental errors, and are approximately 2 μM (Figure 5D, top panel, and Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The XRCC4 and XLF variants have different enthalpic and entropic contributions that compensate one another resulting in similar free energies.
source: Nevertheless, the XRCC4 and XLF variants have different enthalpic (ΔH0, dark grey bars) and entropic (-TΔS0, light grey bars) contributions (Figure 5D, bottom panel, and Table 1) that compensate one another resulting in similar free energies (ΔG0, black bars).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Figure 5D and Table 1.

claim: The stoichiometry of the XRCC4 and XLF interaction is 1:1 for all variants.
source: Also, ITC experiments showed that for all variants (and conditions) the stoichiometry of the XRCC4 and XLF interaction is 1:1 (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: The Kd measured with full-length (WT) proteins is about half of that measured for XRCC4 and XLF truncations missing the disordered tails.
source: In fact, the Kd measured with full-length (WT) proteins is about half of that measured for XRCC4 and XLF truncations missing the disordered tails (Malivert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited research.

claim: The XRCC4-Ala variants combined with either XLF-WT or XLF-Ala variants modestly enhanced ligation as compared to the WT counterpart.
source: The XRCC4-Ala variants combined with either XLF-WT or XLF-Ala variants modestly enhanced ligation as compared to the WT counterpart (Figure 6, lanes 5, 6, 8, and 9) suggesting more stable DNA-protein complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T4 ligase assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Stimulation of T4 ligase activity is minimal with the Asp mutants, most dramatically when aspartate mutants of both XRCC4 and XLF are utilized concomitantly.
source: In contrast, stimulation of T4 ligase activity is minimal with the Asp mutants; this is most dramatic when aspartate mutants of both XRCC4 and XLF are utilized concomitantly (Figure 6, lanes 13).
evidence: This is demonstrated by T4 ligase assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: When both XRCC4-Asp and XLF-Asp variants are combined, DNA bridging activity is severely impaired.
source: When both XRCC4-Asp and XLF-Asp variants are combined, DNA bridging activity is severely impaired (Figure 7, lanes 18).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA bridging assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: The ability of the XLF-Asp variant to bridge long DNA on its own is strongly reduced.
source: Of note, the ability of the XLF-Asp variant to bridge long DNA on its own is also strongly reduced (Figure 7B, lane 8) although its ability to bind to DNA is not affected when tested by EMSA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA bridging assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: XRCC4-WT efficiently binds DNA only when flushed at high concentrations, but once bound, the protein remains stably attached to DNA.
source: We observed that XRCC4-WT efficiently binds DNA only when flushed at high concentrations, but once bound, the protein remains stably attached to DNA (Figure 8B, left panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: XLF's association with DNA is much faster than XRCC4, but XLF also dissociates faster from DNA than XRCC4.
source: As compared to XRCC4, XLF's association with DNA is much faster, but XLF also dissociates faster from DNA than XRCC4 (Figure 8B, middle panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: When WT XRCC4 and XLF are mixed together at an equimolar ratio, a strong enhancement of DNA association is observed followed by dissociation with comparable kinetics to XLF alone.
source: When WT XRCC4 and XLF are mixed together in solution, at an equimolar ratio, and flushed, a strong enhancement of DNA association was observed followed by dissociation with comparable kinetics to XLF alone (Figure 8B, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: XRCC4-WT's association rate is at least 10-times slower than that of XLF-WT alone or that of the XRCC4-WT + XLF-WT combination.
source: Nevertheless, we estimate that XRCC4-WT's association rate is at least 10-times slower than that of XLF-WT alone or that of the XRCC4-WT + XLF-WT combination.
evidence: This is an estimate based on SPR data analysis.

claim: XRCC4's dissociation rate is at least 10-times slower than that of XLF-WT alone or in combination with XRCC4-WT.
source: Moreover, also XRCC4's dissociation rate is at least 10-times slower than that of XLF-WT alone or in combination with XRCC4-WT.
evidence: This is an estimate based on SPR data analysis.

claim: The combination of the two Asp variants resulted in a 4-fold drop in the equilibrium affinity as compared to the WT-WT combination.
source: In contrast, the combination of the two Asp variants resulted in a 4-fold drop in the equilibrium affinity as compared to the WT-WT combination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The initial rapid dissociation phase (koff_fast) was accelerated 4-fold in the case of the XRCC4-Asp + XLF-Asp complexes as compared to the WT-WT complexes.
source: The slower dissociation kinetic component (koff_slow) was similar for all combinations of XRCC4 and XLF variants, but, interestingly, the initial rapid dissociation phase (koff_fast) was accelerated 4-fold in the case of the XRCC4-Asp + XLF-Asp complexes as compared to the WT-WT complexes (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The decrease in equilibrium affinity detected for the XRCC4-Asp + XLF-Asp complexes can be explained by the increase in the rate of dissociation without a major change in the rate of association.
source: Thus, the decrease in equilibrium affinity detected for the XRCC4-Asp + XLF-Asp complexes can be explained by the increase in the rate of dissociation without a major change in the rate of association of XRCC4-Asp + XLF-Asp complexes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SPR data analysis.

claim: Simultaneous aspartate substitutions within the C-terminal tails of both XRCC4 and XLF results in a shifted DNA binding equilibrium, such that complexes bind to DNA similarly to WT XRCC4/XLF complexes, but detach much faster.
source: Taken together, these analyses indicate that simultaneous aspartate substitutions within the C-terminal tails of both XRCC4 and XLF results in a shifted DNA binding equilibrium, such that complexes bind to DNA similarly to WT XRCC4/XLF complexes, but detach much faster.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SPR experiments.

claim: Alanine or aspartate modifications have no major impact on LIG4 activity, even when LIG4-XRCC4-Asp was combined with XLF-Asp.
source: As can be seen, alanine or aspartate modifications have no major impact on LIG4 activity, even when LIG4-XRCC4-Asp was combined with XLF-Asp.
evidence: This is demonstrated by LIG4 ligation assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: The disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF regulate the DNA bridging activity of XRCC4-XLF complexes, but do not directly affect the ability of XLF to stimulate the XRCC4/LIG4 complex.
source: These data suggest that the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF regulate the DNA bridging activity of XRCC4-XLF complexes, but do not directly affect the ability of XLF to stimulate the XRCC4/LIG4 complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LIG4 ligation assays.

claim: XLF is dispensable for V(D)J recombination in murine lymphocytes.
source: Although XLF is dispensable for V(D)J recombination in murine lymphocytes, XLF is required for V(D)J recombination in human lymphocytes, and patients with mutations in XLF exhibit a SCID phenotype (Buck et al., 2006; Woodbine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: XLF is required for V(D)J recombination in human lymphocytes.
source: Although XLF is dispensable for V(D)J recombination in murine lymphocytes, XLF is required for V(D)J recombination in human lymphocytes, and patients with mutations in XLF exhibit a SCID phenotype (Buck et al., 2006; Woodbine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Patients with mutations in XLF exhibit a SCID phenotype.
source: Although XLF is dispensable for V(D)J recombination in murine lymphocytes, XLF is required for V(D)J recombination in human lymphocytes, and patients with mutations in XLF exhibit a SCID phenotype (Buck et al., 2006; Woodbine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: In 293 T cells lacking both XRCC4 and XLF, transfection of the XRCC4 only encoding construct does not reconstitute either coding or signal joining.
source: Thus, in 293 T cells lacking both XRCC4 and XLF, transfection of the XRCC4 only encoding construct does not reconstitute either coding or signal joining
evidence: This is demonstrated by V(D)J recombination assays shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Substantial complementation is observed for both coding and signal end joining when both XRCC4 and XLF are expressed in 293 T cells lacking both proteins.
source: in contrast, substantial complementation is observed for both coding and signal end joining when both XRCC4 and XLF are expressed (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by V(D)J recombination assays shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Expression constructs encoding XRCC4-XLF with 14 phosphorylation sites substituted to either Ala or Asp fully reconstitute both V(D)J coding and signal end joining.
source: As can be seen, the expression constructs encoding XRCC4-XLF with 14 phosphorylation sites substituted to either Ala or Asp fully reconstitute both V(D)J coding and signal end joining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by V(D)J recombination assays shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Phospho-mimetic or -blocking mutations in the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF do not affect joining of RAG-induced DSBs of episomal substrates.
source: We conclude that phospho-mimetic or -blocking mutations in the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF do not affect joining of RAG-induced DSBs of episomal substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the V(D)J recombination assays.

claim: DSBs introduced by restriction enzymes can be repaired by a-NHEJ, although this repair is slower, less efficient, and requires terminal short sequence homology.
source: In contrast to RAG induced DSBs that are exclusively dependent on c-NHEJ for repair, DSBs introduced by restriction enzymes can be repaired by a-NHEJ, although this repair is slower, less efficient, and requires terminal short sequence homology (Deriano and Roth, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Some end joining is observed in cells lacking both XRCC4 and XLF, reflecting a-NHEJ activity.
source: As can be seen in Figure 10B, some end joining is observed in cells lacking both XRCC4 and XLF, or in cells complemented with only XRCC4; this reflects a-NHEJ activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by I-Sce1 end joining assays shown in Figure 10B.

claim: End joining is much more efficient when both XRCC4 and XLF are expressed.
source: However, end joining is much more efficient when both XRCC4 and XLF are expressed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by I-Sce1 end joining assays shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Blocking or phospho-mimicking the 14 sites does not affect the efficiency of end joining of I-Sce1 induced DSBs on episomal substrates.
source: As with RAG-induced DSBs, blocking or phospho-mimicking the 14 sites does not affect the efficiency of end joining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by I-Sce1 end joining assays shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Stable XRCC4/XLF DNA bridging is not required for efficient end joining of proximal I-Sce1 or RAG induced DSBs on episomal substrates.
source: All together from these data, we conclude that stable XRCC4/XLF DNA bridging is not required for efficient end joining of proximal I-Sce1 or RAG induced DSBs on episomal substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the episomal end joining assays.

claim: XRCC4 is required not only to stimulate LIG4, but is also required for LIG4 stability.
source: XRCC4 is required not only to stimulate LIG4, but is also required for LIG4 stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The LIG4 mutant XRCC4-XLF construct does not enhance end joining.
source: As can be seen (Figure 11), the LIG4 mutant XRCC4-XLF construct does not enhance end joining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by I-Sce1 end joining assays shown in Figure 11.

claim: DNA bridging by XRCC4-XLF complexes does not promote a-NHEJ.
source: These data suggest that DNA bridging by XRCC4-XLF complexes does not promote a-NHEJ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the I-Sce1 end joining assays with the LIG4 mutant.

claim: A marked shift in XRCC4's electrophoretic mobility is induced by zeocin at 1 or 24 hr post treatment in cells expressing WT but not Ala XRCC4 and XLF.
source: As can be seen (Figure 12B), a marked shift in XRCC4's electrophoretic mobility is induced by zeocin (at 1 or 24 hr post treatment) in cells expressing WT but not Ala XRCC4 and XLF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The shift in XRCC4's electrophoretic mobility induced by zeocin is equivalent to the change in mobility observed in the XRCC4 Asp mutant.
source: The shift is equivalent to the change in mobility observed in the XRCC4 Asp mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting shown in Figure 12B.

claim: WT XRCC4 and XLF substantially reverse both zeocin and neocarzinostatin sensitivity of 293T XRCC4/XLF deficient cells.
source: As can be seen (Figure 12C and D), WT XRCC4 and XLF substantially reverse both zeocin and neocarzinostatin sensitivity of 293T XRCC4/XLF deficient cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays shown in Figure 12C and D.

claim: In 293 T cells, blocking all 14 phosphorylation sites with alanine substitutions reduces cell survival after exposure to either zeocin or neocarzinostatin compared to cells expressing WT controls.
source: In 293 T cells, blocking all 14 phosphorylation sites with alanine substitutions reduces cell survival after exposure to either zeocin or neocarzinostatin compared to cells expressing WT controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays shown in Figure 12C and D.

claim: The Asp variants combination does not reverse either zeocin or neocarzinostatin sensitivity in XRCC4/XLF deficient 293 T cells.
source: In contrast, the Asp variants combination does not reverse either zeocin or neocarzinostatin sensitivity in XRCC4/XLF deficient 293 T cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays shown in Figure 12C and D.

claim: In 293 T cells, XRCC4-XLF stable DNA bridging is required for repair of zeocin and neocarzinostatin induced DSBs.
source: These data suggest that in 293 T cells, XRCC4-XLF stable DNA bridging (abrogated in the Asp mutants combination) is required for repair of zeocin and neocarzinostatin induced DSBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell survival assays.

claim: Disassembly of XRCC4-XLF complexes is required to facilitate repair of zeocin and neocarzinostatin induced DSBs.
source: Moreover, the fact that the Ala variants combination is also impaired suggests that disassembly of XRCC4-XLF complexes is also required to facilitate repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell survival assays.

claim: In HCT116 cells, both the Ala and Asp variants fully reconstitute zeocin resistance.
source: In HCT116 cells, both the Ala and Asp variants fully reconstitute zeocin resistance (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: In HCT116 cells, cells expressing either Asp or Ala mutants are more sensitive to neocarzinostatin than WT controls.
source: In contrast, cells expressing either Asp or Ala mutants are more sensitive to neocarzinostatin (the drug inducing more dramatic end aberrations) than WT controls (Figure 12—figure supplement 1, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different organisms and different cell types have variable dependence on XLF.
source: Thus, as we and others have shown previously (Li et al., 2008; Roy et al., 2015), different organisms, and different cell types have variable dependence on XLF.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: In XR-1 XRCC4/XLF double deficient cells, whereas WT XRCC4 and XLF substantially reverse neocarzinostatin hypersensitivity, complementation is progressively less substantial with the Ala and Asp variant constructs.
source: Similar, to 293 T cells, whereas WT XRCC4 and XLF substantially reverse neocarzinostatin hypersensitivity, complementation is progressively less substantial with the Ala and Asp variant constructs (Figure 12—figure supplement 2, right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chromosomal deletions are readily detected with both gRNA pairs in cells that have been reconstituted with XRCC4 and XLF.
source: As can be seen, chromosomal deletions are readily detected with both gRNA pairs in cells that have been reconstituted with XRCC4 and XLF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCR amplification shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Certain DSBs may be more readily joined by a-NHEJ than other DSBs.
source: Although no joints are observed in the vector control cell strain with one gRNA pair, deletional joints are observed with the other suggesting that certain DSBs may be more readily joined by a-NHEJ than other DSBs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chromosomal deletion experiments.

claim: The deletional joints using gRNAs 2 and 3 (that induce the small 300 bp deletion) appear remarkably similar in cells expressing WT, Ala, and Asp versions of XRCC4 and XLF by electrophoretic mobility.
source: By electrophoretic mobility, the deletional joints using gRNAs 2 and 3 (that induce the small 300 bp deletion) appear remarkably similar in cells expressing WT, Ala, and Asp versions of XRCC4 and XLF (Figure 13B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCR amplification shown in Figure 13B.

claim: Joints recovered from cells expressing WT or alanine substituted XRCC4 and XLF are very similar for the 4 kb deletion.
source: By sequence analyses, joints recovered from cells expressing WT or alanine substituted XRCC4 and XLF are very similar.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis of chromosomal joints.

claim: Joints recovered from cells lacking XRCC4 and XLF display increased nucleotide loss.
source: As expected, joints recovered from cells lacking XRCC4 and XLF display increased nucleotide loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13C and D.

claim: Joints from all four cell strains predominately occur at regions of short end terminal homology (SSH).
source: Although joints from all four cell strains predominately occur at regions of short end terminal homology (SSH), the length of SSH is increased in cells lacking XRCC4 and XLF (Figure 13C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13C.

claim: The length of SSH is increased in cells lacking XRCC4 and XLF.
source: Although joints from all four cell strains predominately occur at regions of short end terminal homology (SSH), the length of SSH is increased in cells lacking XRCC4 and XLF (Figure 13C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13C.

claim: Joints recovered from cells expressing aspartate substituted XRCC4 and XLF show an intermediate increase in nucleotide loss.
source: Joints recovered from cells expressing aspartate substituted XRCC4 and XLF show an intermediate increase in nucleotide loss, and moderate increase in the length of SSH utilized in joining (Figure 13D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13D.

claim: Joints recovered from cells expressing aspartate substituted XRCC4 and XLF show a moderate increase in the length of SSH utilized in joining.
source: Joints recovered from cells expressing aspartate substituted XRCC4 and XLF show an intermediate increase in nucleotide loss, and moderate increase in the length of SSH utilized in joining (Figure 13D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13D.

claim: DNA bridging facilitates accurate repair of certain chromosomal DNA DSBs.
source: We conclude that DNA bridging facilitates accurate repair of certain chromosomal DNA DSBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chromosomal deletion and sequence analysis experiments.

claim: Blocking or mimicking DNA-PK/ATM phosphorylated residues in the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF impacts on the stability of XRCC4/XLF complexes.
source: Here we report that blocking or mimicking DNA-PK/ATM phosphorylated residues in the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF impacts on the stability of XRCC4/XLF complexes, which are readily dismantled from DNA when DNA-PK/ATM sites are phospho-mimicked.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: XRCC4/XLF complexes are readily dismantled from DNA when DNA-PK/ATM sites are phospho-mimicked.
source: Here we report that blocking or mimicking DNA-PK/ATM phosphorylated residues in the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF impacts on the stability of XRCC4/XLF complexes, which are readily dismantled from DNA when DNA-PK/ATM sites are phospho-mimicked.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: ATM/DNA-PK phosphorylation of XRCC4/XLF filaments facilitates their dissociation from DNA.
source: We propose that ATM/DNA-PK phosphorylation of XRCC4/XLF filaments facilitates their dissociation from DNA.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: XRCC4 and XLF can form alternating filamentous structures that can further assemble into bundles with a central channel.
source: Structural and docking studies have revealed that XRCC4 and XLF can form alternating filamentous structures that can further assemble into bundles with a central channel (Andres et al., 2012; Hammel et al., 2011; Ropars et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited structural studies.

claim: When interacting with DNA, XRCC4-XLF complexes would wrap around DNA, trapping it in the central channel forming a tube-like structure that can diffuse along the DNA with very little friction.
source: One model proposes that when interacting with DNA, XRCC4-XLF complexes would wrap around DNA, trapping it in the central channel forming a tube-like structure that can diffuse along the DNA with very little friction (Brouwer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a model proposed in cited research.

claim: DNA tethering by XRCC4-XLF bundles would be promoted by the ability of XRCC4 dimers to tetramerize by interdigitation of their α-helical stalks.
source: DNA tethering by these bundles would be promoted by the ability of XRCC4 dimers to tetramerize by interdigitation of their α-helical stalks (Andres et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited structural studies.

claim: XLF alone is able to bridge DNA when the size of the DNA molecule is increased (2.7 kb instead of 0.5 kb).
source: Here, we find that XLF alone is able to bridge DNA when the size of the DNA molecule is increased (2.7 kb instead of 0.5 kb, Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DNA bridging assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: A single XLF dimer interacts with, thus bridges, two independent DNA molecules.
source: Given that XLF is a dimer where each monomer has a single DNA binding domain located within the very last ~20 residues of the C-terminus (Andres et al., 2007), we propose that a single XLF dimer interacts with, thus bridges, two independent DNA molecules.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on structural knowledge and experimental data.

claim: The XLF DNA binding domain is akin to the 'AT-hook' DNA binding motifs present in High Mobility Group A proteins.
source: The XLF DNA binding domain is akin to the 'AT-hook' DNA binding motifs present in High Mobility Group A proteins; these AT-hook motifs are all similar to XLF's C-terminal tail in that they are intrinsically disordered DNA binding protein domains (Aravind and Landsman, 1998; Fonfría-Subirós et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on cited literature comparing DNA binding domains.

claim: The AT-hook motif is a weak DNA binding module interacting with the minor groove of DNA preferentially with AT rich regions.
source: The AT-hook motif is a weak DNA binding module interacting with the minor groove of DNA preferentially with AT rich regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AT-hook motifs.

claim: Phosphorylation of XRCC4 on T233 by CDK2 has been implicated in recruitment of PNK, Aprataxin, and APLF through interaction with the FHA domain present in these DNA processing enzymes.
source: Phosphorylation of XRCC4 on T233 by CDK2 has been implicated in recruitment of PNK, Aprataxin, and APLF through interaction with the FHA domain present in these DNA processing enzymes, thus affecting the scaffold function of XRCC4 (Cherry et al., 2015; Clements et al., 2004; Iles et al., 2007; Koch et al., 2004; Macrae et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of XLF by Akt on T181 triggers its dissociation from the LIG4/XRCC4 complex and its sequestration in the cytoplasm.
source: Phosphorylation of XLF by Akt on T181 triggers its dissociation from the LIG4/XRCC4 complex and its sequestration in the cytoplasm (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: DNA-PK phosphorylation of XRCC4 in vitro reduces its affinity for DNA.
source: Although DNA-PK phosphorylation of XRCC4 in vitro reduces its affinity for DNA (Modesti et al., 1999), neither XRCC4 nor XLF DNA-PK/ATM dependent phosphorylations are required for c-NHEJ as measured by complementation of radiosensitivity or V(D)J joining assays in living cells (Lee et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2003, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Neither XRCC4 nor XLF DNA-PK/ATM dependent phosphorylations are required for c-NHEJ as measured by complementation of radiosensitivity or V(D)J joining assays in living cells.
source: Although DNA-PK phosphorylation of XRCC4 in vitro reduces its affinity for DNA (Modesti et al., 1999), neither XRCC4 nor XLF DNA-PK/ATM dependent phosphorylations are required for c-NHEJ as measured by complementation of radiosensitivity or V(D)J joining assays in living cells (Lee et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2003, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: DNA-PK autophosphorylation sites exist as a functional cluster where ablation of one or two sites had no functional impact.
source: We have reported previously that DNA-PK autophosphorylation sites exist as a functional cluster; in these studies, ablation of one or two sites had no functional impact.
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors.

claim: The functional impact of DNA-PK autophosphorylation could only be appreciated when most or all of the sites in the cluster were abrogated.
source: The functional impact of phosphorylation could only be appreciated when most or all of the sites in the cluster were abrogated (Cui et al., 2005; Ding et al., 2003; Neal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior research by the authors.

claim: Co-expression of XRCC4 and XLF phospho-mimetic variants in XRCC4/XLF double deficient cells failed to fully rescue cellular sensitivity to neocarzinostatin.
source: Consistent with a functional role in DNA bridging of chromosomal DSBs, co-expression of XRCC4 and XLF phospho-mimetic variants in XRCC4/XLF double deficient 293 T cells, HCT116 cells, or XR-1 cells failed to fully rescue cellular sensitivity to neocarzinostatin — even though these complexes can stimulate LIG4/XRCC4 activity in vitro and join both RAG or I-Sce1-induced DSBs on episomal substrates in living cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays in the study.

claim: DNA bridging is required to repair neocarzinostatin induced chromosomal DNA DSBs.
source: We conclude that DNA bridging is required to repair neocarzinostatin induced chromosomal DNA DSBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell survival assays.

claim: Rejoined chromosomal DSBs from cells that cannot form XRCC4/XLF filaments display increased nucleotide loss.
source: This conclusion is bolstered by results presented in Figure 13 demonstrating that rejoined chromosomal DSBs from cells that cannot form XRCC4/XLF filaments (because of phospho-mimicking substitutions) display increased nucleotide loss, and a higher dependence on short sequence homology at the DNA termini.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13.

claim: Rejoined chromosomal DSBs from cells that cannot form XRCC4/XLF filaments display a higher dependence on short sequence homology at the DNA termini.
source: This conclusion is bolstered by results presented in Figure 13 demonstrating that rejoined chromosomal DSBs from cells that cannot form XRCC4/XLF filaments (because of phospho-mimicking substitutions) display increased nucleotide loss, and a higher dependence on short sequence homology at the DNA termini.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 13.

claim: Co-expression of XRCC4 and XLF phospho-blocking mutants in XRCC4/XLF double deficient cells only partially reversed sensitivity to neocarzinostatin.
source: Moreover, co-expression of XRCC4 and XLF phospho-blocking mutants in XRCC4/XLF double deficient cells only partially reversed sensitivity to neocarzinostatin providing evidence that phosphorylation-dependent disruption of XRCC4 and XLF complexes is also very important for repair.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell survival assays in the study.

claim: Phosphorylation-dependent disruption of XRCC4 and XLF complexes is very important for repair.
source: Moreover, co-expression of XRCC4 and XLF phospho-blocking mutants in XRCC4/XLF double deficient cells only partially reversed sensitivity to neocarzinostatin providing evidence that phosphorylation-dependent disruption of XRCC4 and XLF complexes is also very important for repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell survival assays.

claim: Dismantle of XRCC4-XLF-DNA complexes after repair is complete is a crucial step in c-NHEJ.
source: We suggest that dismantle of XRCC4-XLF-DNA complexes (after repair is complete) is a crucial step in c-NHEJ, perhaps analogously to the recently established requisite release of the Ku ring after completion of repair (Brown et al., 2015; Postow, 2011; Postow et al., 2008; van den Boom et al., 2016), and that is tightly regulated by phosphorylation of the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF, possibly by DNA-PK/ATM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Dismantle of XRCC4-XLF-DNA complexes is tightly regulated by phosphorylation of the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF, possibly by DNA-PK/ATM.
source: We suggest that dismantle of XRCC4-XLF-DNA complexes (after repair is complete) is a crucial step in c-NHEJ, perhaps analogously to the recently established requisite release of the Ku ring after completion of repair (Brown et al., 2015; Postow, 2011; Postow et al., 2008; van den Boom et al., 2016), and that is tightly regulated by phosphorylation of the disordered C-terminal tails of XRCC4 and XLF, possibly by DNA-PK/ATM.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.
